title: "Avatar", a Modified Ex vivo Work Loop Experiments Using In vivo Strain and Activation
protocol: Select in vivo strain trajectory for use during ex vivo work loop experiments.
Measure time, length or strain, EMG/activation, and force data from in vivo dynamic locomotion.
Segment the entire in vivo trial into individual strides using a programming platform.
Plot length changes versus time for the entire in vivo trial to visualize individual strides.
Calculate strain for the entire trial (Length (L) / Maximum Isometric Force at Optimal Length L0).
Select a stride representative of all strides that begins and ends at similar lengths.
Compare each stride visually by graphing lengths on top of each other.
Segment out strain, EMG/activation, and force data from the entire trial.
Interpolate data points if sampling frequencies differ among variables.
Calculate the frequency of segmented strides by dividing 1 second by the duration of a stride.
Determine how many data points are required in ex vivo experiments to match the frequency.
Calculate the time required for two strides.
Repeat strides at least once to estimate within-muscle measurement error.
Determine the phase of stimulation relative to strain input using measured EMG activity.
View EMG signal over the same x-axis range as strain change.
Enlarge the EMG signal to be visible by rescaling in MATLAB or other software.
Determine where EMG activity starts and stops based on a change in intensity of two standard deviations.
Calculate the percentage of the strain cycle at which EMG activation onset occurs.
Calculate the duration of EMG stimulation considering excitation-contraction coupling delays specific to each animal and muscle.
Prepare representative strain inputs for the work loop controller program.
Interpolate the selected stride to capture two cycles at in vivo frequency.
Rescale the stride to start and stop at "zero strain" after stretching by a pre-determined length excursion.
Select a length excursion for mouse EDL stretching without causing damage.
Set up equipment and surgery for ex vivo work loop experiments.
Prepare a tissue-organ bath by inserting the oxytube needle valve into the water-jacket tissue bath.
Connect the oxytube to a gas cylinder containing 95% O2 and 5% CO2.
Allow 20 psi to fill the water-jacket tissue bath.
Run an additional oxytube from the gas line to a crystallizing dish filled with Krebs-Henseleit solution near the surgery area.
Prepare 1 L of Krebs-Henseleit solution containing (in mmol l-1): NaCl (118); KCl (4.75); MgSO4 (1.18); KH2PO4 (1.18); CaCl2 (2.54); and glucose (10.0) at room temperature.
Adjust pH to 7.4 using HCl and NaOH.
Fill the bath with Krebs-Henseleit solution at room temperature and pH 7.4.
Submerge the muscle and the hook completely in the solution.
Turn on all equipment; dual-mode muscle lever system, stimulator, and signal interface (DAQ board).
Deeply anesthetize the mouse.
Perform euthanasia by cervical dislocation.
Lay the mouse in either a right or left lateral recumbent position with the top hindlimb stretched and toes touching the dissection board.
Remove the fur from the ankle to above the knee joint.
Tent the skin with forceps and cut from the ankle joint to the hip area.
Cut around the ankle like a "hem" of pants.
Pull the skin up to expose the leg muscles more clearly.
Locate the fascia line separating the tibialis anterior (TA) and gastrocnemius.
Separate using dissection scissors to expose the knee tendons.
Place dissection scissors between the two exposed knee tendons.
Blunt dissect a pocket while pulling the scissors away from the leg until reaching the ankle to expose the EDL.
Lace one end of size 4-0 silk surgical suture under the tendon closest to the knee.
Tie a double square knot above the proximal muscle-tendon junction without placing it on the muscle or including the tendon.
Cut above the knot.
Gently pull the loop tied to the tendon, and the EDL will emerge from the pocket.
Tape the loop to the dissection area to create tension in the EDL.
Tie a double square knot using another pre-tied loop knot at the distal muscle-tendon junction without placing it on the muscle or including the tendon.
Cut the knot on the side closer to the leg to remove the whole EDL from the mouse.
Cut the extra suture away from the double square knots on the proximal and distal sides of the muscle.
Place the muscle in the aerated bath by the surgery area.
Attach the EDL muscle vertically between suspended platinum electrodes on the servomotor lever rig.
Attach the distal loop knot to the stationary hook and attach the proximal loop knot to the hook attached to the servomotor arm.
Raise the tissue bath to submerge the muscle in aerated Krebs-Henseleit solution.
Allow the muscle to equilibrate for 10 minutes before beginning stimulation.
Measure the maximum isometric force of EDL muscle.
Stimulate the muscle with a supramaximal twitch (80 V, 1 pps, 1 ms) to ensure no damage occurred during surgery.
Use the length knob on the muscle lever system to find a muscle length using twitch stimulation at which active tension is ~1V / 0.1271 N and passive tension is less than ~0.1V / 0.01271N.
Record the starting length of the muscle from suture knot to suture knot in volts and millimeters.
Input measurements into the calibration portion of the program for starting length.
Find supramaximal twitch maximum isometric force at optimal length (L0) of EDL.
Wait 1 min between stimulations to stabilize passive tension.
Record the length in Volts at which the supramaximal twitch is maximum.
Measure the muscle from suture knot to suture knot at this length.
Shorten the muscle back to starting length with active tension ~1V / 0.1271 N.
Find supramaximal tetanus maximum isometric force of EDL (80 V, 180 pps, 500 ms).
Record the length in Volts and millimeters at which the supramaximal tetanic force occurs.
Measure the muscle fibers from suture knot to suture knot again with calipers.
Find submaximal isometric force of EDL (45 V, 110 pps, 500 ms) at L0 before and after the experiment.
Ensure fatigue did not occur by checking for a 10% decrease in force.
Increase or decrease length by 0.50 V to find passive tension of 1 V.
Rest 3 min between changing length by 0.50 V.
Increase or decrease length by 0.50 V to find passive tension of ~1 V.
Rest 3 min between changing length by 0.50 V.
At length of L0.
Set up the software necessary to complete "avatar" work loop techniques.
Return to L0 after experiment and measure L0.
Complete the avatar work loop technique.
Upload scaled strain changes and length excursion into the program from step 1.4.
Adjust the starting length of the muscle if needed.
Input the starting length in V and mm to calibrate results.
Use stimulation onset and duration calculated in step 1.3.
Run the muscle through two cycles of scaled length changes with determined length excursion.
Save data after each cycle.
Wait 3 minutes between each stimulation protocol on the same muscle.
Stimulate at optimal length (L0) using submaximal activation to determine fatigue.
If force decreases by more than 10%, consider muscles fatigued.
Remove the muscle from the bath when testing is complete.
Cut-loop knots from the muscle and dab off excess solution.
Weigh the muscle after removing it from the bath.
Determine physiological cross-sectional area using the standard formula: muscle mass/(L0*1.06).
Tune parameters for "avatar" work loop technique as needed.
Determine the starting length and length excursion by matching ex vivo passive tension rise to in vivo passive tension rise.
Choose three starting lengths, for example -5% L0, L0, and +5% L0.
Perform an "avatar" work loop at each of these starting lengths with a specified length excursion, such as 10% L0.
Repeat the process with new starting lengths and/or excursions until the rate of ex vivo passive tension rise is similar to in vivo passive tension rise.
Depending on fiber types and activation dynamics of the muscles used, increase or decrease the duration of stimulation to optimize the match between ex vivo and in vivo force production.
Change the onset and/or duration of stimulation as necessary to best match in vivo force production during "avatar" experiments.
